Designed for GitHub Copilot. Because Copilot does not support the MCP protocol, this file focuses more on CLI command references to help Copilot understand how to coordinate with Backlog.md shell commands during code generation. Located under .github/, it only takes effect in GitHub repositories.
Instruction File Content
All generated instruction files follow a unified content framework, mainly including the following modules.
Workflow Guide
Explains the recommended workflow for AI collaborating with Backlog.md:

Load project reality first: in a new session, before giving any answer or plan, run commands such as backlog config list, backlog search , backlog task list, backlog task view , and backlog overview to read the actual statuses, defaultStatus, defaultAssignee, and active tasks.
Do not assume the default status set [To Do, In Progress, Done]; when setting or validating task statuses, they must fall within the configured statuses.
defaultStatus must be a member of statuses; if not, prompt the user to fix or choose another default.
How to read tasks via CLI or MCP.
How to write an implementation plan before implementation.
How to complete tasks step by step according to acceptance criteria.
How to add a final summary and mark the task complete.


This "load reality first" rule is written in the overview guide distributed with the CLI (rather than the project's own AGENTS.md), so it applies to any project using Backlog.md.

The loading cadence for backlog instructions overview is once per session: the guide instructs the agent to run this command once at the start of the session, before giving any answer or taking action; there is no need to repeat it within the same session after it has been read.
References and Line-Number Positioning
The guide specifies that task References support line-number references. Each reference is one of three forms: external URL, project-relative file path, or path with a line range (path:LINE for a single line, path:START-END for a continuous range). The references / addReferences / removeReferences parameters in task creation/editing and MCP follow the same convention; removeReferences matches by the full stored string (including the line-number suffix). Document links similarly distinguish three target types: external URL, Backlog short link (/task/:id, /doc/:id, etc., with optional line-number suffix), and project-relative path.
Date and Multi-Line Input Conventions
The guide also clarifies two common high-frequency input mistakes:

Date and time fields: CLI and MCP accept local-time input, store it as UTC, and convert back to local time for display. Do not read the UTC value visible in the task file and pass it back as input, or a time-zone offset will be introduced.
Multi-line text fields: use literal \n inside quotes to represent newlines; do not press the actual Enter key inside quotes—the shell will split it into multiple lines and only the first line will be saved.

Task Creation Conventions
Defines standards for high-quality tasks:

Title should concisely summarize the task purpose.
Description should focus on "why" rather than "how".
Acceptance criteria must be outcome-oriented and verifiable.
Each task corresponds to an independent Pull Request.

Acceptance Criteria Format
Details the format requirements for acceptance criteria:

Use numbered checkbox form - [ ] #1 criteria content.
Add via CLI --ac parameter.
Manage completion status via --check-ac and --uncheck-ac.
Support operating on multiple criteria items in a single command.

Command Reference
Provides a complete CLI command quick-reference table, covering:

Task create, edit, view, archive
Acceptance criteria and DoD management
Search and filtering
Document and decision management
Board and overview

backlog instructions Volumes
In addition to writing instruction files into the project, the CLI has a built-in set of printable workflow volumes that correspond one-to-one with MCP resources:
backlog instructions            # print volume index
backlog instructions --list     # list available volumes
backlog instructions overview   # print a specific volume




Volume
Description




overview
Workflow overview; must-read before answering any user request; renders the full state machine based on current project configuration at the end


task-creation
How to search, scope, and create tasks


task-execution
How to plan, update, and advance tasks


task-finalization
How to verify, summarize, and complete work


milestones
How to create, edit, remove, and archive milestones


documents
How to create, update, list, and view project documents


decisions
How to create and list decisions, including output modes and status handling


drafts
How to create, promote, demote, and archive drafts


memos
How to create, list, view, update, and delete quick memos


init-required
How to initialize Backlog.md in the current directory (fallback guide for uninitialized projects)




The overview volume carries the project state machine; when printed, it is assembled on the fly from the current config.yml, not a static text (doc-19 FR-8).

MCP vs. CLI Instruction Approach
Backlog.md supports two AI integration approaches, each with applicable scenarios:



Dimension
MCP Approach
CLI Instruction Approach




How it works
AI directly calls Backlog.md tool functions
AI reads instruction files and then executes shell commands on its own


Reliability
High—parameters and return values are structured data
Medium—depends on AI parsing shell output


Supported tools
Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Kiro, Cursor
GitHub Copilot, Cursor


Configuration complexity
Low—one command completes registration
Low—instruction files are generated automatically


Real-time feedback
Immediate—results returned right after tool call
Delayed—must wait for shell command execution


Error handling
AI can precisely obtain error type and cause
AI must infer errors from stderr



Recommended strategy:

If the AI tool you use supports MCP, prefer the MCP approach.
For tools such as GitHub Copilot that do not support MCP, use the CLI instruction approach as a supplement.
Cursor supports both MCP and AGENTS.md instruction files; choose either or use both.
The two approaches can coexist: MCP handles daily task management, while CLI instruction files ensure Copilot, Cursor, and others also understand project conventions.

50-AI集成/03-Wiki Skill 安装.html.title: Wiki Skill Installation
50-AI集成/03-Wiki Skill 安装.html.body:
Wiki Skill Installation
Backlog.md includes the llm-wiki-for-backlog skill to help AI agents understand and maintain the project knowledge base. Use the backlog wiki install command to install this skill into supported AI tools with one click.
What Is the Wiki Skill
llm-wiki-for-backlog is an Agent Skill that provides the following capabilities:

Build knowledge base: automatically generate a structured wiki from project backlog content.
Incremental ingestion: compile new tasks, documents, and decisions into cross-referenced knowledge pages.
Query and report: answer project-related questions based on wiki content.
Health check: scan for contradictions, orphan pages, and missing references in the knowledge base.

After installation, AI agents can directly reference the skill's guide during sessions and perform wiki-related operations more accurately.
Supported AI Tools



Alias
Corresponding Tool
Skills Directory




claude
Claude Code / Claude Desktop
.claude/skills/


codex
OpenAI Codex CLI
.codex/skills/


agents
Generic agents directory
.agents/skills/



Installing the Skill
Install to a Specific Agent
backlog wiki install claude

This command writes the built-in skill files into the agent's skills directory. The installation result shows the skill name, description, and trigger words.
Force Overwrite
If the target directory already contains a skill with the same name, or the directory is occupied by another skill, use --force to overwrite:
backlog wiki install claude --force

Preview Installation
Use --dry-run to preview the installation without actually writing files:
backlog wiki install codex --dry-run

Installation Mechanism
Unified Storage and Symbolic Links
Skill files are centrally stored in .agents/skills/llm-wiki-for-backlog/ at the project root. Each agent's skills directory uses a symbolic link pointing to this unified location:
.agents/skills/llm-wiki-for-backlog/     ← actual files
.claude/skills/llm-wiki-for-backlog/    ← symbolic link
.codex/skills/llm-wiki-for-backlog/     ← symbolic link
The benefits of this design are:

Updating the skill only requires modifying one place.
Multiple agents share the same skill content.
File duplication and version inconsistency are avoided.

Windows Compatibility
Creating directory symbolic links on Windows requires administrator privileges or developer mode to be enabled. When symbolic link creation fails, the command automatically falls back to direct copying of files into the agent's actual directory and logs a warning.
Skill Source
Skill content is embedded into the compiled binary at build time:

Canonical source: .codex/skills/llm-wiki-for-backlog/SKILL.md
Embedded artifact: src/skills/embedded/llm-wiki-for-backlog.ts
Build-time generation: scripts/embed-wiki-skill.ts packages the skill files as a TypeScript module.

This means the compiled backlog binary can install the skill even without network access or the source repository.
Updating the Skill
After upgrading Backlog.md, the built-in skill content may have been updated. Re-run the install command to overwrite to the latest version:
backlog wiki install claude --force

It is recommended to check and update installed skills after each Backlog.md upgrade (the method for upgrading the CLI itself is in the "Upgrade Backlog.md" section of Installation & Initialization).
Post-Installation Workflow
After installing the skill, AI agents can maintain the project wiki according to the llm-wiki-for-backlog conventions. It is not RAG—it does not re-derive knowledge on every query. Instead, it incrementally compiles backlog sources into a persistent, interlinked wiki, with knowledge accumulating over time. The four agent-side operations are:



Operation
Description




Ingest
Read backlog sources such as tasks/, docs/, decisions/, generate source summary pages, concept pages, and entity pages, and update index.md / overview.md / log.md; when git is available, perform incremental ingestion based on changes since the last ingest.


Query
Read wiki/index.md first, synthesize answers from the compiled wiki, and write products (reports, etc.) to wiki_output/.


Lint
Scan for contradictions, orphan pages, stale claims, and missing cross-references.


Flowback
Save valuable query results back into wiki/ to let knowledge compound.



Maintenance boundaries (consistent with the WIKI GUIDELINES in AGENTS.md):

wiki/ is fully maintained by the LLM—human-readable and browsable, but do not edit by hand; hand edits will be overwritten by the next ingest and break interlink consistency.
Backlog source directories (tasks/, docs/, etc.) are read-only for wiki operations.
Ingest never recursively processes wiki/ or wiki_output/ itself.
wiki/log.md is append-only; all cross-page references use wikilinks (page, without .md).

Related

Migration Skill Installation — install the task-migration-architect skill (backlog migrate install) for upstream change analysis and task-driven branch merging.

50-AI集成/04-Migration Skill 安装.html.title: Migration Skill Installation
50-AI集成/04-Migration Skill 安装.html.body:
Migration Skill Installation
Backlog.md includes the task-migration-architect skill to help AI agents analyze upstream changes in forked projects and complete branch merges in a task-driven way. Use the backlog migrate install command to install this skill into supported AI tools with one click. The installation mechanism is the same as Wiki Skill Installation.
What Is the Migration Skill
task-migration-architect is an Agent Skill that provides the following capabilities:

Upstream change analysis: use git log / git show to verify upstream changes and assess their impact on the fork.
A/B/C classification: classify upstream differences into direct port, adapted port, and deliberate exclusion.
Task-driven branch merging: turn migration items into backlog tasks and implement and verify them one by one.
Exclusion list maintenance: record upstream changes deliberately excluded by this fork through a project memory file to avoid repeated evaluation.

Supported AI Tools



Alias
Corresponding Tool
Skills Directory




claude
Claude Code / Claude Desktop
.claude/skills/


codex
OpenAI Codex CLI
.codex/skills/


agents
Generic agents directory
.agents/skills/



Installing the Skill
Install to a Specific Agent
backlog migrate install claude

Force Overwrite
If the target directory already contains a skill with the same name, use --force to overwrite:
backlog migrate install claude --force

Note: --force only overwrites skill content files and does not overwrite project memory files (see seed-only semantics below).
Preview Installation
Use --dry-run to preview the installation without actually writing files:
backlog migrate install codex --dry-run

Project Memory File (Seed-Only Semantics)
The skill includes a project memory file references/current-branch-migration-exclusions.md for recording the list of upstream changes excluded by this fork. It is project-private memory and is handled differently from skill content files:

Only the template is embedded in the binary (current-branch-migration-exclusions.template.md content).
On first install, a copy of the template is written with the formal file name as a starting point.
If the target file already exists, it is always skipped—even with --force it will not overwrite the list you maintain in the project.

Installation output clearly distinguishes two groups: Project memory seeded (template; never overwritten) (newly written seeds this time) and Project memory kept (already exists) (memory files preserved because they already exist).
Exclusion List Bootstrap
If the exclusion list is still an unfilled template after installation, the skill has a built-in bootstrap flow: the AI agent will guide you to fill in the first version of the exclusion list based on the project's actual situation, after which the project maintains it itself. The skill also includes MIGRATION GUIDELINES injection guidance, which can write migration conventions into the project's AGENTS.md in an idempotent marker style.
Installation Mechanism
Same as wiki install: skill files are centrally stored in .agents/skills/task-migration-architect/, and each agent's skills directory points to this unified location via symbolic links; on Windows, when symbolic link creation fails, it automatically falls back to direct copying. Skill content is embedded into the compiled binary at build time, so installation works in offline environments. See the "Installation Mechanism" section of Wiki Skill Installation for details.

70-快速笔记/00-Memos简介.html.title: Memos Overview
70-快速笔记/00-Memos简介.html.body:
Memos Overview
Memos (quick notes) are the fifth file entity in Backlog.md, designed for one-off casual notes: a meeting conclusion, a critical log snippet during debugging, or a fleeting idea. Previously anything worth remembering had to become a task or document—even a single-line meeting record had to fit the ID scheme, title, and paragraph structure. Memos make "write it down now, decide later" possible.
Differences from Other Entities




Tasks / Drafts
Documents / Decisions
Memo




Purpose
Executable, trackable work items
Formal knowledge assets
Lightweight capture inbox


ID
back-123 / draft-3
doc-5 / decision-3
20261003-1 (date + daily sequence)


Title
Required
Required
No title; derived from first body line


Structural requirements
Status, acceptance criteria, and other metadata
Type, directory organization
Body only + optional tags



Memos are deliberately lightweight: no status flow, no milestones, no acceptance criteria, and they do not enter the dependency graph (Graph View). Their value lies in outbound connections—bare entity IDs and path written in the body automatically become links, turning casual notes into growable nodes of the knowledge network (see Search & Knowledge Linking).
Storage Format
All memos are saved under the backlog/memos/ directory, one Markdown file per note:
---
id: 20261003-1
created_date: 2026-10-03 01:14
updated_date: 2026-10-03 01:14
tags: [meeting]
---

Weekly meeting conclusion: v2 release delayed by one week; fix performance regressions first. Related task back-123.


ID rule: YYYYMMDD-N format; N is the max existing memo sequence of the day + 1, resetting to 1 across days.
Frontmatter: only id, created_date, updated_date, and optional tags (omitted when the tag list is empty); there is no title field.
Card title: derived from the first non-empty line of the body; if the body starts with blank lines, falls back to the first 40 characters.
Temporary data: backlog/memos/ is treated as a temporary capture area and is deliberately not version-controlled by default (adjust .gitignore yourself if you want to keep them).

Four Entry Points
The same storage is shared by four surfaces, with identical ID scheme and file format:

CLI: backlog memo create/list/view/update/delete, the fastest terminal capture path. See CLI Memo Commands.
Web: the /memos page stream for quick capture + calendar mode. See Web Memo Page.
MCP: memo_create / memo_list / memo_view / memo_update / memo_delete tool group, directly readable and writable by AI agents.
HTTP API: /api/memos* routes (list, calendar counts, read/write by ID) for scripts and third-party tools.

In addition, memos are integrated into Global Search; the CLI provides backlog instructions memos usage guide, and the MCP side provides the backlog://workflow/memos workflow resource.
Usage Recommendations

Capture lightly: one memo says one thing; write it and forget it, relying on search and links to find it later.
Use tags: use --tags or inline #tag in the Web UI to create coarse-grained partitions of the inbox.
Write entity IDs: casually include IDs like back-123, doc-5 in the body; they automatically become links when rendered.
Digest regularly: memos are an inbox, not a destination; important conclusions should be promoted to tasks or documents. This release does not provide an automatic promotion path; the bridging method is to reference the memo ID in a task body.

70-快速笔记/01-CLI备忘命令.html.title: CLI Memo Commands
70-快速笔记/01-CLI备忘命令.html.body:
CLI Memo Commands
The backlog memo subcommand group provides fast capture and browsing in the terminal. It shares the same storage module (src/core/memos.ts) with the HTTP API and MCP tools, ensuring a single ID scheme and a single file format.
Creating Memos
# Inline creation (memo create does not accept positional arguments; body must use --content)
backlog memo create --content "Weekly meeting conclusion: v2 release delayed by one week" --tags meeting

# Multi-line content read from stdin (when --content is omitted)
cat debug.log | backlog memo create --tags debug

# Manual multi-line input: type the body directly in the terminal, end with EOF
backlog memo create --tags debug
# Type the memo, then end with Ctrl+D (Ctrl+Z on the classic Windows console). Ctrl+C aborts.
# First line
# Second line


In an interactive terminal, omitting --content enters keyboard capture: prompts go to stderr (so they do not mix into the body), and multiple lines are written as-is. Ctrl+C aborts without creating a file (exit code 130). Ending input with an empty body reports Memo content is empty. and does not create a file.
End key: prefer Ctrl+D—VS Code integrated terminal, Git Bash, and Windows Terminal all pass this key to the program as-is, and on Unix/macOS/WSL it produces a real EOF. The classic Windows console (cmd/PowerShell) does not deliver any EOF, so use Ctrl+Z instead; note that Ctrl+Z is intercepted in VS Code and is a suspend signal in mintty (Git Bash), so use Ctrl+D uniformly in those two environments.
Implementation note: in TTY mode the command switches to raw mode to recognize these keys, so echo is handled by the CLI itself (character-by-character echo, Enter for new line, Backspace to erase the current line). In pipe/redirect mode it remains "read stdin directly, no echo".


--content : inline body; when omitted, read from stdin—direct read for pipes/redirects, keyboard capture in TTY.
--tags : comma-separated tag list; effective in both input modes.
On success, the CLI prints the new memo ID (such as 20261003-1).

Listing Memos
backlog memo list

# View memos for a specific day only
backlog memo list --date 2026-10-01

# Filter by tags (comma-separated or repeatable, case-insensitive, any match)
backlog memo list --tags meeting,debug

The list outputs the latest first, one line per memo as "ID + one-line preview" (first 20 characters of the body, newlines removed, truncated with ellipsis). Use memo view for the full text.
List Paging
memo list supports the same unified paging window options as other list commands:



Option
Description
Example




--max-count 
Output at most n items
--max-count 20


--skip 
Skip the first n items (next page)
--skip 20


--count
Output only the total match count (a single number)
--count



Truncated text output ends with Showing - of  items. Next: backlog memo list --skip ; copy it to page forward. --count outputs only a number and cannot be combined with --json. The centralized explanation of paging semantics for list commands is in the "List Paging" section of Search & Sequences.
Plain-Text Output
backlog memo list --plain

--plain outputs a plain-text list, good for AI agents and scripts to parse. Note: CLI text search output (backlog search) does not include memo results—memos are treated as Web-only types (consistent with Wiki results); JSON output carries memo summaries.
Viewing a Memo
# TTY environment: open scrollable viewer (PageUp / PageDown to page)
backlog memo view 20261003-1

# Non-TTY or --plain: print full text and frontmatter directly
backlog memo view 20261003-1 --plain

Updating a Memo
# Replace the body
backlog memo update 20261003-1 --content "Corrected conclusion"

# Append a line (preserves existing content)
backlog memo update 20261003-1 --append "Supplement: performance regression located in cache layer"

# Change only tags (body unchanged)
backlog memo update 20261003-1 --tags meeting,important

# Change body and tags together
backlog memo update 20261003-1 --append "Add one sentence" --tags meeting,important

# Clear tags
backlog memo update 20261003-1 --tags ""

--content and --append are mutually exclusive; --tags can be combined with either or used alone (changing only tags is a valid update). Providing none of the three errors with No update options provided. and exits. Omitting --tags leaves the original tags unchanged; passing an empty value --tags "" clears tags. Updates refresh updated_date.
Tag parsing is consistent with REST PATCH /api/memos/:id: trim, drop empty items, deduplicate, and support comma-separated or repeated input (--tags a --tags b). Note that memos have no title; modifying the first non-empty line of the body changes the card title shown in lists.
Deleting a Memo
backlog memo delete 20261003-1

Deletion success prints a confirmation; a non-existent ID is reported clearly.
Viewing the Usage Guide
The CLI has a built-in memos usage guide:
backlog instructions memos

This guide covers parameters, filtering, paging semantics, and not-found error handling for all subcommands. AI agents read it along with configuration on first load.

70-快速笔记/02-Web备忘页面.html.title: Web Memo Page
70-快速笔记/02-Web备忘页面.html.body:
Web Memo Page
After starting the Web interface, the Memos entry in the sidebar (expandable list + collapsed icon bar) opens the /memos page. The page provides both feed and calendar modes within the same component, sharing the same selected date and deep-linkable via the ?view= parameter.
Feed Mode
Feed is the default view of /memos: a quick-capture composer at the top, and a reverse-chronological stream of memo cards below.
Quick Capture

The top composer reuses the same editor as Rich-Text Paste: supports pasting images, dragging in files, and Word document conversion; pasted images are automatically promoted to assets/paste/ before saving.
Click the save button or press Cmd/Ctrl+Enter to save; the new memo is immediately pinned to the top without refreshing.
On save failure, the note content is preserved and a localized error banner is shown; it is not silently lost.

Card Stream

Cards show creation time, rendered body (Markdown, Mermaid diagrams, wiki links, and auto-linked entity IDs), and read-only tag chips. Entity ID ranges (such as back-101~105) and slash lists (such as back-101/102/103) in the body are rendered as a single trigger; clicking opens a portal dropdown listing each clickable ID in the range.
The tag bar uses a single-line folded historical tag strip: recently used tags are compressed into one line, active tags are pinned to the top, and clicking expands filtering options. Cards support inline editing, archiving, and deletion (archiving is detailed in Pinboard View & Archiving). Typing #topic# in the composer (such as #login#) tags the memo's topic without polluting the body; this closed syntax is recognized as a topic tag.
Infinite scroll automatically loads subsequent pages based on an IntersectionObserver sentinel; memo changes are broadcast via WebSocket memos-updated and synced in real time across all open tabs.

Pinboard Mode
/memos also has a third view—a WebGL sticky-note pinboard: ?view=board goes directly there. Notes have fixed landing spots, the blackboard stays fixed without scrolling, and it supports full-screen; hovering over a note shows archive options, and clicking opens the edit popup. See Pinboard View & Archiving for details.
Calendar Mode
Click the view toggle to enter calendar mode: a CSS Grid month view with intensity-gradient coloring by daily memo count (data from GET /api/memos/calendar), today highlighted, with no third-party calendar library dependency.

Month navigation: prev / next / today buttons flip months across years and refetch counts; the first and last days of adjacent months are dimmed in the grid.
Select a day: clicking a day expands a DayPanel below the grid in place (no page navigation), listing all memos for that day, with inline editing or deletion.
Backfill historical dates: the DayPanel has its own composer; memos written there are pinned to the selected date via createdDate (the ID prefix is derived accordingly), suitable for post-meeting notes.
View in feed: a panel action sets selectedDate as a date-filter chip and switches back to feed mode—"select a day to filter the feed, clear the chip to return to all".
Deep link: ?view=calendar&date=YYYY-MM-DD goes directly to that month, preselects that day, and auto-expands the panel.

Integration with Global Search
The "Memos" tab in the global search dialog searches memos; clicking a result row jumps to the day view at /memos?date= (memos do not have an independent detail route). See Global Search and Search & Knowledge Linking.
Interface Language
All copy on the Memos page (capture hints, calendar buttons, error banners, etc.) is covered in en / zh-CN / zh-TW / ja and switches instantly with the interface language setting.

70-快速笔记/03-搜索与知识互联.html.title: Search & Knowledge Links
70-快速笔记/03-搜索与知识互联.html.body:
Search & Knowledge Linking
Memos' two core values—findable and connected—are provided by global search integration and outbound knowledge-network links. Both reuse existing pipelines without introducing new parsing code just for memos.
Global Search Integration
Memo is the fifth result type in global search, alongside tasks, drafts, documents, decisions, and Wiki:

The Web search dialog provides a "Memos" filter tab; results are grouped by type with icons and group labels consistent with other types; clicking a result row jumps to the /memos?date= day view.
The server-side /api/search type whitelist includes memo (previously only four types; it used to reject type=memo).
CLI: backlog search --json output adds the memo summary shape; plain-text output skips memos (treated as Web-only types, consistent with Wiki results).

Because memos deliberately do not enter the ContentStore snapshot, the search index reads the backlog/memos/ corpus directly through an injected loader. Refresh is controlled by a "stat signature + 500ms corpus TTL" double gate: when the signature has not changed, only a lightweight directory scan is performed and re-reading is skipped; when the signature changes (add/modify/delete), the index is rebuilt in full in the background (reload does not block the current search). Therefore newly captured memos after startup are searchable without restarting the service: the first search after the background reload completes hits them; the search that triggered the reload may still return old results.
Outbound Knowledge Network Links
Memo bodies are rendered through the shared MermaidMarkdown renderer and automatically gain two existing linking mechanisms:

Bare entity IDs: IDs written in the body such as back-123, doc-5, decision-3 are automatically converted to clickable links via the entity index, opening the corresponding entity with client-side navigation.
Wiki links: path (supporting alias alias syntax) are parsed as Wiki page links.
IDs inside inline code are not rewritten; IDs that cannot be uniquely resolved are displayed as plain text.
ID ranges and slash lists: ranges like back-101~105 and slash lists like back-101/102/103 are also recognized and rendered as a single expand trigger; the dropdown lists links for each ID in the range. The #topic# closed syntax is recognized as a topic tag rather than an entity link.

Thus a casually written "related task back-123" becomes a live link in the Web interface, and a range like back-101~105 can be expanded to the whole interval with one click.
Outbound Only, Not Inbound
By design, memos are not link targets: there is no /memo/:id detail route, memo is not included in the entity-type union, and memo-to-memo links are not supported. This is a deliberate trade-off—memos are a lightweight inbox, not permanent nodes in the knowledge network; content that needs to be referenced should be promoted to a task or document.
Real-Time Sync
Memo writes from any entry point (CLI, Web, MCP, HTTP API) broadcast a memos-updated WebSocket event: the /memos page instantly refreshes the card stream and calendar counts, while other pages handle it through their own data refresh pipelines. Search index refresh does not use this broadcast; it is triggered by the signature + TTL double-gate mechanism described above.

70-快速笔记/04-钉板视图与归档.html.title: Pinboard View & Archiving
70-快速笔记/04-钉板视图与归档.html.body:
Pinboard View & Archiving
In addition to feed and calendar, /memos provides a third view—the pinboard: all memos appear as yellow sticky notes pinned to a blackboard, suitable for glancing at the distribution and pile-up of all notes at once.
Entering the Pinboard
Switch to the pinboard view on the /memos page (URL parameter ?view=board deep-links directly). In pinboard mode, the quick-capture composer and tag filter bar are automatically hidden; the blackboard area is fixed and fills the container, without scrolling with the page. A button in the upper-right corner can make the blackboard full-screen (the blackboard itself goes full-screen; popups and buttons remain visible inside it). If the browser does not support WebGL, a hint is shown in the blackboard area instead of a blank page.
Sticky Note Rendering Rules
Each sticky note's position and appearance is deterministic: paper variant, pin color, tilt angle, and landing spot are derived from the memo ID hash, so refreshing the page never reshuffles the layout. Each sticky note has a fixed height (about 150px); when content overflows, it is truncated with an ellipsis at the end, so long memos do not infinitely expand the pinboard or cover neighboring notes. Notes near the board edges naturally overlap, and notes underneath can still be discovered by hovering or clicking.
Sticky Note Interactions

Hover: the note lifts and floats to the top layer; an archive button appears in the upper-right corner.
Click: press and release on the note to open the note popup—the popup content has the same editing experience as the feed card (body, tags, save, delete), and the title is the first line of the note.
Archive: click the archive icon that appears on hover, or choose Archive from the card menu after closing the popup—the note/card disappears from the board and feed.

Archiving Notes
Archiving moves the note file from backlog/memos/ to backlog/archive/memos/; the note content is preserved unchanged. Archiving is one-way: the current version has no unarchive entry point and no archive browsing view; archived notes no longer appear in the feed, calendar counts, tag filtering, or pinboard. When creating a new project, backlog init creates both the memos and archive/memos directories.

80-图谱与数据查询/00-图谱CLI命令.html.title: Graph CLI Commands
80-图谱与数据查询/00-图谱CLI命令.html.body:
Graph CLI Commands
The backlog graph command group lets you run read-only Cypher queries against the project's task/knowledge graph directly from the terminal, and also create your own named databases, write data, and import from CSV. It is the command-line counterpart to the Web interface Cypher search (the magnifying-glass dialog in backlog browser), suitable for ad-hoc analysis, scripting, and pipeline output. The complete official guide is always available:
backlog instructions graph


Queries are strictly read-only: write keywords (CREATE / DROP / DELETE / INSERT / MERGE / SET / UPDATE) are rejected; neither the graph nor the Markdown corpus is modified. Run from the project root (or a subdirectory) so the CLI can locate backlog/.

Backend and Performance

Backend status: the default backend is RyuGraph WASM (Kuzu's MIT fork built for WebAssembly), executing inside Bun's WebAssembly runtime and working out of the box on all platforms without any environment variables. The native Kuzu dependency has been removed; BACKLOG_GRAPH_BACKEND=kuzu is no longer a valid value. BACKLOG_GRAPH_BACKEND=memory forces a pure-JS memory fallback mode (Cypher search is not supported). If ryu initialization fails, it automatically falls back to the memory backend without crashing, and prints a one-line English warning explaining the failure path and cause (database path not visible to the WASM filesystem means MEMFS cannot see the path; engine error means an engine-level failure—only the latter needs to be reported). The database itself lives in the WASM in-memory filesystem, while the cache directory only stores locks and fingerprint sidecars; this is normal.
Snapshot reuse: the first run of a default graph command requires a full build (about 6–11 seconds for this repository); the CLI writes the build result as a JSON snapshot to the OS cache directory. After that, as long as the corpus fingerprint, parser version, and graph-structure version have not changed, it restores directly from the snapshot (about twice as fast). When the corpus changes, it automatically rebuilds and refreshes the snapshot. Snapshots are only a cache; deleting them only costs one rebuild.
Each invocation is independent: each CLI run opens the database in memory and closes it on exit, not contending with the graph held by the Web interface (each uses independent slots and locks).

Database Concepts
Each subcommand operates on a database name:

default: the graph derived from Markdown corpus (tasks, drafts, milestones, Wiki, documents, decisions). It is a read-only cache; any write operation is rejected and prompts you to use graph create instead.
User databases: created with backlog graph create; data is persisted as JSON snapshots under /databases/ (can be version-controlled with the project) and is readable/writable across processes.

backlog graph list                              # list default and all user databases (with sizes)
backlog graph create people "people and their relationships"   # create a user database
backlog graph describe people                   # view description, timestamp, and per-table row counts for a database
backlog graph drop people                       # delete a database and its snapshot (default cannot be deleted)

Viewing the Schema
backlog graph schema default          # print node tables (with properties and primary keys) and relationship tables (with endpoints)
backlog graph schema default --json   # machine-readable JSON

schema has the alias show-schema. The default graph's node tables are FileNode (one node per Markdown file, properties include path / id (uppercase task ID) / type / title / status / updatedDate), Tag, and Meta (internal bookkeeping, meaningless for queries); relationship tables are ParentOf (parent → child), BelongsToMilestone (task → milestone), DependsOn (dependent → dependency), SourcedFrom, LinksTo, and TaggedWith. Note that the node label is FileNode, not File.
Running Cypher Queries
backlog graph query default "MATCH (n:FileNode) RETURN count(n)"
backlog graph query default "MATCH (a:FileNode)-[:ParentOf]->(b:FileNode) RETURN a.path, b.path LIMIT 10"
backlog graph query people "MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(b:Person) RETURN a.name, b.name"


The first positional parameter is the database name, and the second is the Cypher statement (wrap it in quotes; double quotes work across platforms). The old single-argument form backlog graph query "MATCH ..." is still valid and equivalent to querying default.
Default output is an aligned plain-text table (no ANSI escapes, safe for pipes); --json outputs the raw result object { columns, rows, nodeKeys, truncated } for script consumption.
Interactive display limit is 500 rows; results beyond that include a truncation hint; --all removes this limit and returns all rows.
Task IDs are stored in uppercase. Pay attention to direction when traversing relationships: ParentOf is parent → child, and DependsOn is dependent → dependency.

Writing to User Databases (insert)
backlog graph insert people "CREATE NODE TABLE Person(name STRING PRIMARY KEY, age INT64)"
backlog graph insert people "CREATE REL TABLE KNOWS(FROM Person TO Person)"
backlog graph insert people "CREATE (:Person {name: 'Alice', age: 30})"

insert accepts write Cypher (CREATE / MERGE / SET / DELETE); each successful statement rewrites the snapshot—persistent but not cross-statement transactional. Writes are protected by a per-database single-holder lock and snapshot fingerprint; --force skips fingerprint validation. default rejects insert. Snapshots are whole-database serialization/replay; they work well up to roughly 1e5 rows.
Importing CSV
# Import as nodes: table name defaults to filename; use --node to specify, --map to rename columns
backlog graph import people data/people.csv --node Person --map "First Name=firstName"

# Headerless file: column names auto-generated as column1, column2…
backlog graph import people data/raw.csv --no-header --node Raw

# Import as edges: two columns are the primary keys of the endpoints; endpoints must already exist (matched only, not created)
backlog graph import people data/knows.csv --rel KNOWS --from person --to friend --node Person


The first column is the primary key; importing the same file repeatedly upserts existing rows by primary key and does not produce duplicate edges.
If the table does not exist, it is created automatically and types are inferred from columns (INT64 → DOUBLE → BOOLEAN, fallback STRING); empty cells become NULL.
Malformed files (uneven column counts, unclosed quotes, illegal column names, etc.) report line numbers before opening the database, leaving the database unchanged.
Rows whose endpoints cannot be found during edge import are skipped and the skip count is reported; --from-node / --to-node are only needed when the relationship table does not yet exist.

80-图谱与数据查询/01-图谱MCP工具.html.title: Graph MCP Tools
80-图谱与数据查询/01-图谱MCP工具.html.body:
Graph MCP Tools
The Backlog.md MCP server provides a set of graph_* tools that let AI agents directly query the project's task/knowledge graph and user databases. Their capabilities correspond one-to-one with the CLI backlog graph subcommands. The accompanying MCP usage guide is available through get_backlog_instructions (or the resource backlog://workflow/graph), and mirrors the CLI guide from backlog instructions graph.
Six Tools



Tool
Purpose
Notes




graph_query
Run read-only Cypher against default or a user database, returning columns and rows
readOnlyHint; write keywords (CREATE/MERGE/SET/DELETE/DROP, etc.) are rejected


graph_schema
Return a database's schema: node tables and properties, relationship tables and endpoints
readOnlyHint


graph_list_databases
List default and all user databases with metadata (name, kind, size)
readOnlyHint, no required parameters


graph_describe_database
Return a single database's description, timestamp, and per-table row/edge counts
readOnlyHint


graph_create_database
Create a user database (name + description)
destructiveHint; must explicitly pass acknowledged: true to write


graph_import_csv
Import CSV into a user database: by default imports as nodes (missing tables auto-created with inferred types, upsert by primary key); add rel/from/to to import as edges (endpoints matched but not created)
destructiveHint; files are fully validated before opening the database, so format errors have no side effects



When the database does not exist, query tools return a clear error (and list available databases); write tools always reject the read-only default.
One-Shot Switch Model
Graph MCP tools do not hold a long-lived GraphService: each call goes through a one-shot flow of "open → prepare → execute → close". Specifically:

default uses the derived graph snapshot reuse (same path as the CLI), keeping results consistent with the Web interface.
User databases are hydrated from their JSON snapshots, and write tools re-persist the snapshot after execution.
Therefore agents do not need to manage connections, and there is no contention with the Web server process for the same graph.

Relationship to CLI
Tool parameters correspond to CLI subcommands: graph_query(db, statement) ↔ backlog graph query  [cypher], graph_import_csv(db, csv, …) ↔ backlog graph import  , and so on. Relative paths in graph_import_csv are resolved against the project root, not the MCP process's current directory.

80-图谱与数据查询/02-SQL查询块.html.title: SQL Query Blocks
80-图谱与数据查询/02-SQL查询块.html.body:
SQL Query Blocks
In documents (docs / Wiki and other Markdown), you can embed a read-only query using sqlite-query, duckdb-query, or mdb-query fenced code blocks; the Web interface reading view renders the block as a live query result instead of dead code. In edit mode the original block text is still shown. mdb-query uses an Access database as the data source; its syntax and fields are the same as this page. See MDB Query Blocks for details.
Block Syntax
```sqlite-query
source: backlog/databases/shop.sqlite
view: table
sql: |
  SELECT product, price, stock
  FROM inventory
  ORDER BY price DESC
```




Field
Required
Default
Description




source
Yes
—
Data source path, project-relative (see below)


sql
Yes
—
Query statement; supports multi-line `sql: \
` syntax


view
No
table
table (grid), list (field list per row), value (single value), or echarts (render a chart directly; see Chart Blocks)


refresh
No
manual
Only manual refresh is supported; automatic / scheduled refresh is not supported



Security Constraints and Read-Only Guarantee

source is always resolved as a project-relative path: absolute paths (including leading /), .. escapes, symlinks pointing outside the project, and hidden/excluded directories are rejected. Extensions must be on the whitelist, and SQLite sources are also validated to actually be SQLite files.
SQL must be read-only: it must start with SELECT or WITH … SELECT, no internal semicolons are allowed (a trailing ; is tolerated), and the write-keyword blacklist also applies to comments (a commented-out DROP is still rejected).
The real safeguard is at the engine layer: SQLite is opened with a read-only handle plus PRAGMA query_only, and DuckDB is opened in READ_ONLY mode—even if text validation is bypassed, write operations are rejected by the engine.

Data Sources

sqlite-query: source points to a .sqlite / .sqlite3 / .db file inside the project.
duckdb-query: in addition to .duckdb databases, source can directly point to a CSV / Excel (.csv / .xlsx) file—DuckDB then opens an in-memory instance and queries it directly with FROM 'file.csv'; xlsx relies on the official excel extension auto-loading, which requires an internet download on first use (offline environments show a readable block error). DuckDB blocks also support an optional copy_to field to save results as a csv/xlsx file inside the project.

Row Limit and Pagination

Preview mode displays at most 500 rows by default; when exceeded, a hint "Truncated to N rows (M total)" is shown, and the total row count is reported truthfully.
The limit is configurable via query_max_rows in backlog/config.yml (default 500, hard cap 5000 in preview mode), and can also be changed in the Web settings page under "Query / Data preview".
The block header has a "Paginated browse" toggle: when enabled, results are browsed by page (← Page X / Y →), with rows per page controlled by pagination_page_size (default 50). default_pagination: true can make blocks enter pagination mode by default. Pagination uses true engine-side paging (LIMIT/OFFSET pushdown + separate COUNT(*)), so it is not constrained by the 5000-row limit and is suitable for browsing large result sets.
Both table view and list view show a row-number (# / sequence) column; global row numbers are shown in pagination mode.

Four Block Actions



Action
Description




Refresh
Re-run the query and refresh the results


Show/Hide Query
Expand/collapse the read-only source and SQL panel (collapsed by default; does not issue a request)


Copy Markdown
Copy the current results as a GitHub-flavored Markdown table to the clipboard (value view copies the scalar; NULL becomes an empty cell)


Export CSV
Export the results as a CSV file (UTF-8 BOM + CRLF, Excel can open Chinese directly). SQLite blocks write -.csv next to the database (never overwriting); DuckDB blocks save the file via the browser. Export follows the preview row limit.



The four actions are identical across blocks for all four engines. Changes in the settings page take effect immediately via broadcast without refreshing the page.
Editing Inside Reading View
After expanding the query panel, an edit entry appears at the right end of the first line: in edit mode, the SQL/Cypher statement becomes a syntax-highlighted editor. Click Save to write the new statement back to the source Markdown and re-run immediately, Test to run a dry-run validation without writing to disk, or Discard to restore the original statement. SQL engines also have a Format button to reformat indentation in place (does not write to the file). This feature is common to sqlite-query, duckdb-query, mdb-query, and cypher-query blocks; blocks without a known source path (such as milestone descriptions) remain read-only.

80-图谱与数据查询/04-Cypher查询块.html.title: Cypher Query Blocks
80-图谱与数据查询/04-Cypher查询块.html.body:
Cypher Query Blocks
In documents (tasks / documents / decisions / Wiki and other Markdown), you can embed a read-only Cypher query using a cypher-query fenced code block; the Web interface reading view renders the block as a live query result, while edit mode still shows the original block text. It is the graph-database counterpart to SQL Query Blocks: the interaction semantics and security model are the same, only the execution stack is replaced with a graph engine.
```cypher-query
source: demo
view: graph
refresh: auto
query: |
  MATCH (p:Person)-[r:WORKS_AT]->(c:Company)
  RETURN p, r, c
```




Field
Required
Default
Description




source
Yes
—
Database registered name (a name listed by backlog graph list), not a file path


query
Yes
—
Query statement; supports multi-line `query: \
` syntax; must be read-only


view
No
table
table (grid), list (field list per row), value (single value), graph (force-directed graph), or echarts (render a chart directly; see Chart Blocks)


refresh
No
manual
manual (manual) / auto (re-run automatically when graph data changes)



Unknown fields cause an error and list available fields; they are not silently ignored.
source Is a Registered Name, Not a Path
The source of SQL blocks is a project-relative file path, while Cypher blocks always use a registered name—graph databases are directory-based storage and have no single-file semantics. Unregistered names and any path-like values (relative paths, absolute paths, ..) are rejected; the block shows a readable error and lists available database names.
Four Views



View
Rendering




table
Standard grid, one record per row


list
Each record as a vertical key–value list


value
Only the first row and first cell, inline plain text (good for embedding an aggregate value)


graph
Force-directed graph rendering of nodes and relationships, sharing the same legend configuration as the Databases page



When graph view results exceed about 3000 nodes, it automatically degrades to a table with an explanation. Cypher return values include scalars, nodes, relationships, and paths: nodes are serialized as JSON after stripping internal handles, relationships are rendered as (start)-[type]->(end), and paths are compact strings of alternating nodes and relationships—the graph view uses the raw structure directly.
Live Refresh
refresh: auto subscribes to graph data change broadcasts: after graph content changes, the block automatically re-runs after a short quiet period (500 milliseconds); continuous changes during batch imports trigger only one re-run. When the result is the same as the current value, it does not re-render, avoiding flicker. The block header shows a Live badge and a pause/resume toggle; pausing only stops re-runs. This capability depends on the graph database having change broadcasts—currently only the derived corpus graph has this; writing refresh: auto for user databases behaves the same as manual refresh.
Read-Only Guarantee
Write Cypher (CREATE / MERGE / DELETE / SET / DROP / UPDATE) is rejected and shows an error inside the block; query blocks structurally cannot touch the write path.
Row Limit and Block Actions

The row limit is the same as SQL blocks, taken from the configured query row limit (default 500, hard cap 5000); when exceeded, the block truncates and shows a hint. Cypher does not provide pagination—if the limit is exceeded, change the query rather than paginating.
The four block-header actions are consistent with SQL blocks: Refresh (re-execute), Show/Hide Query (expand/collapse the read-only source and statement, collapsed by default; expanding does not trigger a query; the statement has syntax coloring consistent with the code block), Copy Markdown (copy as GitHub-flavored table), Export CSV (export as a CSV file).
Empty results and errors both have explicit copy; there are no silently blank blocks.

Query Writing Notes
The graph engine currently does not support untyped relationship patterns (-[r]-> matches no rows) or multi-type unions (-[r:A|B]-> errors), so queries must specify concrete relationship types.

80-图谱与数据查询/03-数据库页面.html.url: 80-图谱与数据查询/03-数据库页面.html
80-图谱与数据查询/03-数据库页面.html.title: Databases Page
80-图谱与数据查询/03-数据库页面.html.body:
Databases Page
The Web interface Databases page lists all graph databases in the project—the derived default and all user databases—and provides a read-only Cypher query box scoped to the selected database. The page has no write entry points; the result table is a generic renderer that does not assume the corpus graph schema.
Database List and Real Row Counts

The default row shows the graph service's live count (FileNode + Tag, consistent with the graph page when fully displayed), no longer a "rebuilding" placeholder. The query box answers default directly from the resident in-memory graph and does not trigger corpus rebuild.
The page subscribes to graph change broadcasts (graph-updated); the table refreshes automatically after corpus or database changes.
The query box provides one-click schema examples such as show_tables / table_info (including a "View ALL" one-click full query) and a CLI graph schema hint.

Graph View of Cypher Results
A "Table / Graph / Side-by-side" switch above the result area lets the same query result be read as a table or a graph; the selected mode persists across queries, each new result auto-frames, and returning to an old result restores the previous viewport.

The graph view shares the same canvas interactions as the task/knowledge graph: zoom/pan, hover to highlight neighborhood, click to focus and fly in, node drag, legend toggles. It does not include a Cypher search box (the page already has one), and double-click does not open details (query rows have no detail page).
Internal bookkeeping nodes (Meta table) are hidden by default when other data exists; the legend keeps the entry so it can be restored at any time, and the title indicates the hidden count. Table view is unaffected and still shows all rows.
500 rows is a rendering budget, not a data limit: a checkbox in the query box can remove this limit (equivalent to CLI graph query --all). When result nodes exceed about 3000, the graph pane proactively yields and explains, rather than freezing.
The graph title bar has a full-screen toggle (CSS maximized); a short Esc releases focus, and a long press of 600ms exits maximized.

Configurable Legend
The gear button in the graph pane opens the legend settings panel. Configuration is saved per database in backlog/databases/graph-legends.yaml inside the project (versioned with git) and restored automatically on next visit; the browser also keeps an instant cache and offline copy. The panel is draft-style: changes preview instantly, "Save" writes to disk, and "Cancel" / close / clicking the gear again reverts to the snapshot when opened. Full storage, migration, and hot-update mechanisms are in Legend Configuration Persistence.

Two-layer color model: the first layer determines hue by node type (table label); the second layer distinguishes lightness within a type by a field's subclasses (equal-width bins, quantiles, single threshold, by value, contains, prefix, boolean shortcuts, or hand-written ordered boolean rules). "Generate" one-click produces an editable rule list, with an implicit Other fallback bucket.
Configuration is grouped by node type (accordion panels, one card per type): the title template uses `` placeholders (empty means auto-guess), types can specify explicit colors to override automatic hues, and each rule plus Other can be pinned to a color individually.
Relationships are configured by type with line style (solid / dashed / dotted / long-dash) and arrow (none / end / start / bidirectional), with an optional display name; unconfigured relationship types automatically cycle through line styles.
Each bucket is a legend toggle; after turning it off, the entry remains (grayed out and struck through) and can be turned back on at any time.

80-图谱与数据查询/05-图例配置持久化.html.url: 80-图谱与数据查询/05-图例配置持久化.html
80-图谱与数据查询/05-图例配置持久化.html.title: Legend Persistence
80-图谱与数据查询/05-图例配置持久化.html.body:
Legend Configuration Persistence
Graph view legend configuration (colors per node type, title templates, color rules, and line styles and arrows per relationship) is saved in backlog/databases/graph-legends.yaml inside the project, versioned with git. Previously it only existed in browser local storage, so switching browsers, devices, or clearing cache would lose it, and different team members would see the same graph differently. The coloring of Cypher query blocks (view: graph) in documents even depended on the reader's browser rather than the project itself.
What the Configuration File Looks Like
A single YAML file, grouped by database name:
default:
  captionsVisible: true
  types:
    Person:
      caption: "{{name}}"
      color: "#204af3"
      rules: []
  relations:
    WORKS_AT:
      dash: solid
      arrow: end
      color: "#0ef19a"
  hidden: []

Block-style YAML with LF line endings, easy to review, diff, and edit by hand. Missing fields or broken rules do not crash the interface—reading falls back gracefully.
Four Entry Points, One File



Entry Point
Usage




Legend settings panel
Gear button opens it; changes preview instantly and are written on save


CLI
backlog graph legend get  (default human-readable summary, --json outputs raw JSON) / set   (--stdin reads from standard input) / remove  (idempotent)


MCP
graph_legend_get / graph_legend_set / graph_legend_remove tools; agents do not need to edit files by hand


Manual editing
Edit the YAML directly with an editor



All four paths read and write the same file; changes made anywhere are visible everywhere else.
Startup Recovery and Local Cache
When the browser opens, it first renders using the local cache (zero delay, offline-capable), then fetches the project file from the server:

If the project has a configuration and it differs from local → use the project version and write it back to local cache.
If the project does not have one but local does → upload the local configuration once to complete migration; the old configuration is not lost.
If neither has one → keep the default coloring.

On save, it writes locally first (takes effect immediately) and then writes to the file; if the file write fails, the operation is not interrupted, the local copy is kept, and migration is retried automatically next time the page opens. Behavior is consistent with the pure-local-cache era when the server is unreachable.
Cross-Tab and Out-of-Band Hot Updates
After a legend save, an update is broadcast, and other open tabs of the same project apply it immediately. When the file is modified externally via CLI, MCP, or an editor, the server's file watcher converts the change into the same broadcast—no page refresh needed.
A true change refreshes only once: rewrites with identical content (including only field-order adjustments) do not trigger any refresh; deleting an entry that did not exist is also a silent no-op.
Automatic Colors Are Recorded in the File
On save, colors currently actually drawn for types without an explicit color are written into the file, so the file records the complete picture the viewer sees, rather than leaving it to be re-derived from type names on each open. Clicking the color of a type back to "×" in the panel restores automatic coloring.
Conflict Strategy
Concurrent writes to the same configuration use last-writer-wins, without merging—legend is a low-frequency, single-person configuration. File writes are atomic (temporary file + rename), so no half-written file is left behind.

80-图谱与数据查询/06-图表块.html.title: Chart Blocks
80-图谱与数据查询/06-图表块.html.body:
Chart Blocks
Any Markdown body can embed charts using fenced code blocks: mermaid for flowcharts, sequence diagrams, and Gantt charts; echarts for data charts. The reading view renders them as graphics, while edit mode still shows the source code. Both chart types automatically follow the app's light/dark theme.
Documents, Wiki, memos, tasks, and decisions all use the same rendering chain, so these blocks work in any body.
Flowcharts: mermaid
```mermaid
graph LR
  A[Parse fence] --> B{Language registered?}
  B -->|Yes| C[Render as chart]
  B -->|No| D[Keep code block]
```

Chart Engine Switch (Pele / Mermaid)
Which engine renders mermaid diagrams is now switchable, no longer hard-wired:

Pele (default): open-sourced by the Obsidian team, renders Mermaid 12.1.0 syntax to SVG, zero dependencies; lines and arrows adapt automatically to the theme (dark-mode contrast has been fixed).
Mermaid 11.16.1: kept as an optional fallback engine.

Switch in the Web settings page under Diagram Engine (Pele default / Mermaid); the choice is persisted to project configuration (diagram_engine, default pele) and remains effective after restarting the browser. Both engines affect only Mermaid diagram rendering; ECharts data charts are unaffected.

Want ready-made Mermaid templates? See document doc-32 Mermaid Chart Gallery—18 categories, 25 directly copyable complex examples (flowcharts, sequence diagrams, class diagrams, Gantt charts, ER diagrams, user journeys, mind maps, XY charts, architecture diagrams, etc.), covering project workflows and WeChat/Alipay scenarios.

Data Charts: echarts
The body is standard ECharts option JSON; no new dialect to learn:
```echarts
{
  "title": { "text": "Tasks completed per week" },
  "tooltip": { "trigger": "axis" },
  "legend": {},
  "xAxis": { "type": "category", "data": ["W1", "W2", "W3", "W4"] },
  "yAxis": { "type": "value" },
  "series": [
    { "name": "Completed", "type": "bar", "data": [10, 18, 25, 33] },
    { "name": "New", "type": "line", "smooth": true, "data": [14, 20, 22, 30] }
  ]
}
```

The same series array can mix multiple chart types; the above is a bar chart overlaid with a line chart.
Supported Chart Types
Available values for series[].type:



Category
Types




Cartesian
bar line scatter effectScatter candlestick boxplot heatmap pictorialBar themeRiver


Proportion and flow
pie funnel sankey


Hierarchy and relationships
tree treemap sunburst graph chord


Multi-dimensional and gauges
radar parallel gauge lines



Two exceptions require extra conditions and are not built into the engine:

custom depends on a renderItem function, which JSON cannot express; writing it produces only an empty chart.
map requires GeoJSON registration first, and map data must come from compliant sources, so it is explicitly integrated by the user.

The default coordinate system is Cartesian xAxis / yAxis; polar, singleAxis, calendar, parallel, and geo components are all registered. themeRiver must be paired with singleAxis, and type must be "time", otherwise the river bands do not appear.
Charts Directly from Query Results: view: echarts
Query blocks can draw results directly instead of showing a table. sqlite-query, duckdb-query, and cypher-query all support this by adding view: echarts and a chart field:
```sqlite-query
source: backlog/databases/demo-shop.sqlite
view: echarts
chart: { "type": "bar", "categoryField": "category", "valueField": "revenue", "title": "Revenue by category" }
sql: |
  SELECT category, ROUND(SUM(amount), 2) AS revenue
  FROM order_details GROUP BY category ORDER BY revenue DESC
```

Simple mapping fields:



Field
Description




type
bar / line / pie / scatter / effectScatter


categoryField
Category column; for pie, used as sector name


valueField
Value column


title / name
Chart title / series name, optional


categoryAxisName / valueAxisName
Axis names, optional



For multi-series, dual axes, or custom styles, use the advanced form: write option inside chart and use placeholders for data positions.
```sqlite-query
source: backlog/databases/demo-shop.sqlite
view: echarts
chart: |
  {
    "option": {
      "title": { "text": "Monthly revenue" },
      "tooltip": { "trigger": "axis" },
      "xAxis": { "type": "category", "data": "@result:month" },
      "yAxis": { "type": "value" },
      "series": [{ "type": "bar", "data": "@result:revenue" }]
    }
  }
sql: |
  SELECT substr(ordered_at, 1, 7) AS month, ROUND(SUM(amount), 2) AS revenue
  FROM order_details GROUP BY month ORDER BY month
```

Two placeholders:



Placeholder
Replaced with




"@result"
The entire result set, one {column: value} object per row; suitable for dataset.source


"@result:"
Array of values for that column; suitable for series.data / xAxis.data



Placeholders must appear as whole values, not concatenated into strings; writing a wrong column name yields an empty array.
Referencing Named Query Blocks: fromQuery
When you want both a table and a chart, give the query block an id, then reference it from a separate echarts block:
```sqlite-query
id: monthly
source: backlog/databases/demo-shop.sqlite
sql: |
  SELECT substr(ordered_at, 1, 7) AS month, ROUND(SUM(amount), 2) AS revenue
  FROM order_details GROUP BY month ORDER BY month
```

```echarts
{
  "dataset": { "fromQuery": "monthly" },
  "tooltip": { "trigger": "axis" },
  "xAxis": { "type": "category" },
  "yAxis": { "type": "value" },
  "series": [{ "type": "bar", "encode": { "x": "month", "y": "revenue" } }]
}
```

You can also put the reference on the series itself, directly specifying which two columns to use:
{ "type": "bar", "fromQuery": "monthly", "categoryField": "month", "valueField": "revenue" }

categoryField / valueField are only column-selection instructions on the referencing side and do not remain in the final configuration. When the option has no xAxis, the engine automatically adds a category axis using the first successfully parsed series's categoryField.
Usage Conventions



Aspect
Behavior




Theme
Automatically follows light/dark mode; no configuration needed


Loading
ECharts is loaded on demand, not in the initial bundle


JSON limitation
Only JSON is parsed; function expressions are not executed. Use template strings for dynamic text, such as "{b}: {c}"


Error behavior
On invalid JSON, unknown series type, or missing required fields, the block shows an error or falls back to a code block; it does not crash


Reference scope
fromQuery is only valid within the same document; duplicate ids use the last one


Refresh linkage
When a referenced query re-runs, the chart referencing it automatically redraws; charts without fromQuery are unaffected



For complete chart examples, including copyable configurations and pitfalls for each series type, see document doc-31 ECharts Chart Demo; copy templates for Mermaid diagrams are in document doc-32 Mermaid Chart Gallery.
Related

SQL Query Blocks — fields and read-only constraints for sqlite-query / duckdb-query
Cypher Query Blocks — graph database query blocks, also support view: echarts
Legend Configuration Persistence — color and legend settings for graph views

80-图谱与数据查询/07-MDB查询块.html.title: MDB Query Blocks
80-图谱与数据查询/07-MDB查询块.html.body:
MDB Query Blocks
mdb-query is the fourth live query block for embedding read-only Access (.mdb / .accdb) queries in documents. It shares the same rendering kernel as the sqlite/duckdb engines of SQL Query Blocks and Cypher Query Blocks. The reading view renders the block as a live query result.
Block Syntax
```mdb-query
source: backlog/assets/lizheng.mdb
view: table
sql: |
  SELECT TNMC AS table_name, TNMS AS description
  FROM "g_TableName"
  LIMIT 12
```




Field
Required
Default
Description




source
Yes
—
Access database path, project-relative (no leading /; on Windows /x is treated as an absolute path)


sql
Yes
—
Query statement; supports multi-line `sql: \
` syntax


view
No
table
table / list / value / echarts (render a chart directly; see Chart Blocks)


id
No
—
For echarts blocks to reference via fromQuery (see the linkage explanation in SQL Query Blocks)


refresh
No
manual
Manual refresh only



Engine and Security Model

Access databases are loaded by mdb-reader into an in-memory SQLite instance (PRAGMA query_only=ON), and then executed with the SQLite kernel, so cross-table JOINs and the full SQL surface are supported.
Uses the same four fail-closed gates as sqlite/duckdb: extension whitelist (only .mdb / .accdb), read-only SQL validation (SELECT / WITH shape + keyword blacklist), query_only pragma, and source path escape rejection.
Default result limit is 500 rows; pagination mode is exempt (up to 1000 rows per page).

Chinese Encoding
Old files exported by Windows versions of Access such as Lizheng store text fields as GBK (CP936) bytes. mdb-reader restores them as garbled Latin1, but the mdb-query engine automatically re-encodes them as correct Chinese via GBK before loading into the database. Pure ASCII columns and all numeric columns are already normal and unaffected.
Differences from sqlite/duckdb

No copy_to support: Access files cannot be written in place, so writing copy_to in the block is rejected server-side (only duckdb-query supports it).
Type mapping: long/integer/byte/boolean → INTEGER (boolean displays as 0/1); double/float/single/currency/numeric/decimal → REAL; text/memo/ole/repid/datetime → TEXT (datetime converted to ISO string, ole binary shown as  placeholder); NULL becomes an empty cell.

Inline Editor
mdb-query also supports the in-place editing flow described in SQL Query Blocks: after expanding the query panel, click the edit entry to modify SQL in the reading view, Test to dry-run, and Save to write back to the source document and re-run.
Acceptance Sample
backlog/docs/PRDS/mdb/doc-33 - MDB-Access-Live-Query-演示.md demonstrates all views, read-only interception, path rejection, and fromQuery linkage using the real survey database backlog/assets/lizheng.mdb (87 tables).

60-配置与运维/00-配置管理.html.title: Configuration Management
60-配置与运维/00-配置管理.html.body:
Configuration Management
Backlog.md provides a flexible configuration system, supporting project settings through an interactive wizard or direct command-line management. Configuration is stored in YAML files and version-controlled with project code, ensuring team members use consistent workflow conventions.
Interactive Configuration Wizard
The backlog config command starts the advanced configuration wizard, guiding you through all key settings with interactive questions:
backlog config

The wizard covers the following configuration areas:

Shell completion installation
Cross-branch task status checking
Git hook bypass settings
Auto-commit enablement
ID zero-padding formatting
Default editor selection
Definition of Done (DoD) default items management
Web UI port and auto-open browser

Follow the prompts; each option has a default value and explanatory hint. After configuration completes, Backlog.md automatically writes the settings to the project configuration file.
Direct Command-Line Operations
For quickly modifying a single configuration item, use backlog config get and backlog config set.
Viewing Current Configuration
List all configured items and their current values:
backlog config list

# Plain-text output (unified convention for AI-readable output; byte-for-byte identical to output without the flag)
backlog config list --plain

--plain is listed by the overview guide as the standard way to read live configuration: output is already plain text, and the flag is accepted so that agent invocations that habitually append --plain to every command do not fail with "unknown option".
After the statuses row, config list also prints a derived terminal-status set, such as terminalStatuses: [Done, Dropped] (derived from statuses). Terminal statuses are derived from each status's category (done / dropped) in the state machine; this is read-only presentation, not a settable configuration key—to adjust terminal statuses, modify the corresponding state's category in the state machine editor.
View a single configuration item:
backlog config get projectName
backlog config get statuses
backlog config get defaultPort

Modifying Configuration Items
Set the value of a single configuration item:
backlog config set projectName "My Project"
backlog config set defaultPort 8080
backlog config set autoCommit true

Set list-type configuration items:
backlog config set statuses "To Do,In Progress,Done"
backlog config set labels "bug,feature,docs"


config get/set/list display consistent configuration items through a shared available-keys list. For list-type configurations (statuses, labels), it is recommended to use backlog config get  to view the current value and then edit the corresponding field in config.yml directly (supporting block YAML sequences), rather than overwriting through config set.

Key Configuration Items
Project Basics



Item
Type
Default
Description




projectName
string
—
Project name, displayed on the board and overview


statuses
state-machine object list
Built-in seven-state default machine
Task status flow, ordered (see "State Machine Configuration" below)


labels
string list
—
Project predefined label list


dateFormat
string
—
Date display format


locale
string
en
Web UI language: en, ja, zh-CN, zh-TW


maxColumnWidth
integer
20 (value written by backlog init)
Maximum width of text columns in CLI output; config set only accepts positive integers


milestones
string list
—
Deprecated: milestones now come from milestone files under backlog/milestones/ and are no longer stored in config; config get milestones only lists current milestone IDs and cannot be set (use backlog milestone commands to manage)



The order of the status list determines column order on the board. The first status is treated as the initial task status; terminal statuses are determined by each status's category (done / dropped), no longer simply the last item in the list.
State Machine Configuration
statuses describes the state machine in object form; each status is an object:
statuses:
  - name: To Do
    category: active
    next:
      - to: Planning
        when: Description and acceptance criteria are complete; ready to start
        ai: allowed
  - name: Done
    category: done
    exit: complete
    next: []
  - name: Dropped
    category: dropped
    exit: archive
    display: false
    next: []




Field
Description




name
Status name (required)


category
Category: active / wip / blocked / done / dropped, determines terminal status and completion semantics


exit
Exit action: complete (archive into completed) or archive


next
Array of allowed transition edges; can include when / ai / if / requires / evidence declarations


display
When false, the board hides the column and its tasks (default true)



The legacy string-array format is still compatible (last item is terminal). There is no CLI command to set statuses: it is recommended to maintain it visually in the state machine editor on the Web settings page, or edit this file directly—write the whole object back without losing fields. backlog instructions overview (and the MCP overview resource of the same name) automatically renders a complete readable description of the current state machine. The first backlog init writes the built-in seven-state default machine (To Do / Planning / Plan Review / In Progress / In Review / Done / Dropped, localized with the interface language). Semantic details are in Task Lifecycle.
Task Defaults



Item
Type
Default
Description




defaultAssignee
string list
—
Automatically applied when creating a task/draft without an explicit assignee


defaultEditor
string
code --wait
Editor command used when pressing E to open a task


defaultStatus
string
To Do
Default status used for new tasks when not explicitly specified; should be a status name from statuses


definitionOfDone
string list
—
Project-level Definition of Done default checklist, inherited by new tasks (definition_of_done key in config.yml); cannot be modified via config set, use the interactive wizard, Web settings page, or edit config.yml directly



# Set default assignee (list, comma-separated)
backlog config set defaultAssignee "@alice,@bob"

# Remove default assignee (empty value removes the key)
backlog config set defaultAssignee ""

# Clear default editor—the service default "code --wait" can hang unattended agent processes
backlog config set defaultEditor ""
backlog init --default-editor ""

defaultAssignee follows a three-state semantics:

Not passing -a (field omitted) → apply the configured default assignee.
Explicitly passing -a (even one value) → completely replace the default, not merged.
Explicitly clearing --unassign (or clearing assignee chips in the Web UI) → save as an empty list, no fallback to default.

Defaults are applied at the Core creation-funnel layer, so behavior is consistent across CLI task create, draft create, the creation wizard, TUI N creator, Web POST /api/tasks, and MCP task_create.
Setting defaultEditor to an empty string means "do not use a default editor": config set defaultEditor "" skips executable validation and removes the key, and init --default-editor "" also clears any existing configuration. Non-empty values still validate that the executable exists.
Editor Resolution Priority and Vim / Neovim Configuration
When pressing E to open an editor, resolution priority is (doc-002): EDITOR environment variable > config.yml defaultEditor > platform default (nano on macOS/Linux, notepad on Windows). For Vim / Neovim, setting the environment variable is recommended:
export EDITOR=nvim          # or vim
# Or write to project config
backlog config set defaultEditor nvim


In TUI (backlog board / backlog task ), pressing E suspends the character screen, exits the alternate buffer, and automatically restores terminal state after the editor exits.
Troubleshooting: set TERM=xterm-256color for color issues; editor unresponsiveness or immediate exit usually means the editor path includes arguments—write the full executable path or use a wrapper script.
Per-command override: EDITOR=nvim backlog board.

Branch and Git Integration



Item
Type
Default
Description




checkActiveBranches
boolean
true
Whether to scan other local active branches


includeCrossBranch
boolean
unset (local-first)
Whether scan results enter the board, task list, and search


remoteOperations
boolean
true
Whether to check tasks in remote branches


activeBranchDays
integer
30
Maximum days a branch is considered active


taskResolutionStrategy
string
most_recent (value written by init)
Conflict strategy when tasks with the same name exist in multiple branches: most_recent takes the most recently modified version, most_progressed takes the version whose status has advanced the furthest (falling back to modification time when progress is equal). Runtime falls back to most_progressed when missing. Not in config get/set available keys; configure via Web settings page or config.yml



When checkActiveBranches is enabled, Backlog.md checks other local and remote branches when loading tasks to ensure cross-branch task statuses are accurate. This may affect performance in large repositories; reduce activeBranchDays to speed it up.
includeCrossBranch (corresponding to include_cross_branch in config.yml) controls display: when enabled, the board, task list, and search include tasks that exist only on other branches; when unset, local-first behavior is preserved (historical CLI behavior). It is independent of checkActiveBranches—the latter controls "whether to scan" (and determines the candidate branch set for task ID allocation), while the former controls "whether scan results are displayed". Disabling scanning also narrows the ID allocation candidate set; understand the cost together with activeBranchDays. Both toggles are in the Web settings page Advanced Settings card and take effect immediately without restart.
remoteOperations depends on checkActiveBranches; when the latter is disabled, the former automatically becomes ineffective.
Automation Behavior



Item
Type
Default
Description




autoCommit
boolean
false
Whether to automatically create a Git commit after CLI changes


bypassGitHooks
boolean
false
Whether to bypass Git hooks when committing (using --no-verify)


filesystemOnly
boolean
false
Whether to disable all Git integration and use only the filesystem


onStatusChange
string
—
Callback command executed when a task status changes
